claim: Depletion of CD301b+ DCs specifically enhanced the development of Tfh cells, germinal center B cells and antibody responses against protein antigens.
source: We show here that the depletion of CD301b+ DCs specifically enhanced the development of Tfh cells, germinal center B cells and antibody responses against protein antigens.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing enhanced Tfh, GC B cells, and antibody responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: Exaggerated antibody responses in mice depleted of CD301b+ DCs occurred in the absence of any adjuvants.
source: Exaggerated antibody responses in mice depleted of CD301b+ DCs occurred in the absence of any adjuvants, and resulting antibodies had broader specificity and higher affinity to the immunogen.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data in Figure 3c showing antibody responses to OVA without adjuvant in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: Antibodies generated in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice had broader specificity and higher affinity to the immunogen.
source: Exaggerated antibody responses in mice depleted of CD301b+ DCs occurred in the absence of any adjuvants, and resulting antibodies had broader specificity and higher affinity to the immunogen.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5 showing broader epitope recognition and affinity maturation in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: CD301b+ DCs express high levels of PD-1 ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2.
source: CD301b+ DCs express high levels of PD-1 ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 10a showing PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression on CD301b+ DCs.

claim: Blocking PD-1 or PD-L1 during priming in wild-type mice partially mimicked the phenotype of CD301b+ DC-depleted animals.
source: Blocking PD-1 or PD-L1 during priming in wild-type mice partially mimicked the phenotype of CD301b+ DC-depleted animals, suggesting their role in Tfh suppression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 10 showing enhanced Tfh and GC B cell responses with PD-L1 blockade in WT mice.

claim: Transient depletion of CD301b+ DC results in the generation of autoreactive IgG responses.
source: Transient depletion of CD301b+ DC results in the generation of autoreactive IgG responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6 showing anti-nuclear IgG antibodies in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: CD301b+ DCs play a key role in blocking autoantibody generation.
source: These results revealed a novel regulatory mechanism and a key role of CD301b+ DCs in blocking autoantibody generation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that transient depletion of CD301b+ DCs leads to autoreactive antibody responses (Figure 6).

claim: Dendritic cells are primarily responsible for initiating T cell-mediated cellular immunity.
source: Through presenting processed antigens on their MHC molecules, dendritic cells (DCs) are primarily responsible for initiating T cell-mediated cellular immunity, which is also required for T cell-dependent antibody responses.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about DC function in adaptive immunity.

claim: Follicular helper T cells (Tfh) are marked by their expression of inhibitory receptor PD-1 and chemokine receptor CXCR5.
source: Follicular helper T cells (Tfh) are a subset of CD4+ T cells marked by their expression of inhibitory receptor PD-1 and chemokine receptor CXCR5 and play important roles in the development of GC B cells by providing differentiation, survival and proliferation signals (Crotty, 2011; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Crotty, 2011; Ma et al., 2012).

claim: Tfh cells play important roles in the development of GC B cells by providing differentiation, survival and proliferation signals.
source: Follicular helper T cells (Tfh) are a subset of CD4+ T cells marked by their expression of inhibitory receptor PD-1 and chemokine receptor CXCR5 and play important roles in the development of GC B cells by providing differentiation, survival and proliferation signals (Crotty, 2011; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Crotty, 2011; Ma et al., 2012).

claim: Co-maturation between GC B cells and Tfh is required to stably maintain both subsets.
source: While co-maturation between GC B cells and Tfh is required to stably maintain both subsets (Baumjohann et al., 2013; Deenick et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2008), it has been shown that early instructive signals from antigen-bearing DCs are both necessary and sufficient to prime Tfh differentiation (Baumjohann et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2011; Deenick et al., 2010; Goenka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Baumjohann et al., 2013; Deenick et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2008).

claim: Early instructive signals from antigen-bearing DCs are both necessary and sufficient to prime Tfh differentiation.
source: While co-maturation between GC B cells and Tfh is required to stably maintain both subsets (Baumjohann et al., 2013; Deenick et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2008), it has been shown that early instructive signals from antigen-bearing DCs are both necessary and sufficient to prime Tfh differentiation (Baumjohann et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2011; Deenick et al., 2010; Goenka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Baumjohann et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2011; Deenick et al., 2010; Goenka et al., 2011).

claim: DCs directly support B cell survival and class-switching through their expression of B cell stimulatory ligands such as BAFF and APRIL.
source: For the development of antibody responses, DCs not only promote Tfh differentiation but also directly support B cell survival and class-switching through their expression of B cell stimulatory ligands such as BAFF and APRIL (MacLennan and Vinuesa, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (MacLennan and Vinuesa, 2002).

claim: DCs are important as antigen carriers that provide the initial antigen-specific receptor signaling to the cognate B cells in the lymph nodes.
source: Moreover, DCs are also important as antigen carriers that provide the initial antigen-specific receptor signaling to the cognate B cells in the lymph nodes (LNs) (Qi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Qi et al., 2006).

claim: In vivo antigen delivery to receptors specifically expressed by DCs can trigger robust class-switched antibody production even without an adjuvant.
source: Indeed, in vivo antigen delivery to receptors specifically expressed by DCs can trigger robust class-switched antibody production even without an adjuvant (Chappell et al., 2014; Xu and Banchereau, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Chappell et al., 2014; Xu and Banchereau, 2014).

claim: Antigen delivery strategies targeting distinct DC subsets result in increased antigen-specific antibody titers regardless of the DC subset targeted.
source: Importantly, antigen delivery strategies targeting distinct DC subsets seem to result in increased antigen-specific antibody titers regardless of the DC subset targeted (Lahoud et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2015), suggesting that multiple DC subsets are capable of inducing antibody production (Chappell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Lahoud et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2015).

claim: Multiple DC subsets are capable of inducing antibody production.
source: Importantly, antigen delivery strategies targeting distinct DC subsets seem to result in increased antigen-specific antibody titers regardless of the DC subset targeted (Lahoud et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2015), suggesting that multiple DC subsets are capable of inducing antibody production (Chappell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that different DC subsets can induce antibody responses, supported by citations.

claim: In mouse skin, there are at least three distinct skin-resident DC subsets at the steady-state including epidermal Langerhans cells (LCs), Langerin+ CD103+ dermal DCs (DDCs) and Langerin- CD11b+ DDCs.
source: In mouse skin, there are at least three distinct skin-resident DC subsets at the steady-state including epidermal Langerhans cells (LCs), Langerin+ CD103+ dermal DCs (DDCs) and Langerin- CD11b+ DDCs (Kaplan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Kaplan et al., 2012).

claim: CD301b+ DCs are a major subset of migratory CD11b+ DDCs that express the highest levels of PD-1 ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, among DC subsets in the skin-draining LNs.
source: CD301b+ DCs are a major subset of migratory CD11b+ DDCs that express the highest levels of PD-1 ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, among DC subsets in the skin-draining LNs (dLNs) (Gao et al., 2013; Kumamoto et al., 2009, 2013; Murakami et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Gao et al., 2013; Kumamoto et al., 2009, 2013; Murakami et al., 2013).

claim: CD301b+ DCs are found in the submucosa of gastrointestinal, respiratory and reproductive tract.
source: In addition to the dermis, CD301b+ DCs are found in the submucosa of gastrointestinal, respiratory and reproductive tract (Denda-Nagai et al., 2010; Kumamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Denda-Nagai et al., 2010; Kumamoto et al., 2013).

claim: Inducible depletion of CD301b+ DCs by injecting diphtheria toxin results in impaired Th2 differentiation of antigen-specific CD4+ T cells following footpad immunization of protein antigen with Th2 adjuvants.
source: By using Mgl2-DTR mice in which one of the endogenous Mgl2 alleles (encoding CD301b protein) are replaced with a diphtheria toxin receptor (DTR)-GFP cassette, we have shown previously that inducible depletion of CD301b+ DCs by injecting diphtheria toxin (DT) results in impaired Th2 differentiation of antigen-specific CD4+ T cells following footpad immunization of protein antigen with Th2 adjuvants as well as after subcutaneous infection with Nippostrongylus brasiliensis.
evidence: This refers to previously published work by the authors using the Mgl2-DTR mouse model.

claim: Mice that lack CD301b+ DCs developed intact antibody responses against N. brasiliensis infection despite impaired Th2 differentiation.
source: Notably, despite the impaired Th2 differentiation, mice that lack CD301b+ DCs developed intact antibody responses against N. brasiliensis infection (Kumamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Kumamoto et al., 2013).

claim: CD301b+ DCs are required for IL-17 production from dermal γδT cells following epidermal infection with Candida albicans.
source: In addition, recent studies have expanded the role of CD301b+ DCs beyond the Th2 differentiation program, by demonstrating that they are required for IL-17 production from dermal γδT cells following epidermal infection with Candida albicans, or from Th17 cells with intranasal infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (Kashem et al., 2015b; Linehan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Kashem et al., 2015b; Linehan et al., 2015).

claim: CD301b+ DCs are required for IL-17 production from Th17 cells with intranasal infection with Streptococcus pyogenes.
source: In addition, recent studies have expanded the role of CD301b+ DCs beyond the Th2 differentiation program, by demonstrating that they are required for IL-17 production from dermal γδT cells following epidermal infection with Candida albicans, or from Th17 cells with intranasal infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (Kashem et al., 2015b; Linehan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Kashem et al., 2015b; Linehan et al., 2015).

claim: Immunization of Mgl2-DTR mice depleted of CD301b+ DCs resulted in greatly enhanced production of OVA-specific class-switched antibodies.
source: Immunization of Mgl2-DTR mice depleted of CD301b+ DCs resulted in greatly enhanced production of OVA-specific class-switched antibodies (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b demonstrating increased antibody titers in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: The increased antibody titers were evident on day 14 after a single immunization and enhanced following a systemic secondary exposure to the same antigen without an adjuvant.
source: The increased antibody titers were evident on day 14 after a single immunization and enhanced following a systemic secondary exposure to the same antigen without an adjuvant (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b showing antibody titers at days 14 and 21.

claim: The antibody titers were not elevated when CD301b+ DCs were depleted five days post-immunization.
source: However, the antibody titers were not elevated when CD301b+ DCs were depleted five days post-immunization (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d demonstrating that delayed depletion does not enhance antibody responses.

claim: The presence of CD301b+ DCs during the early phase of primary immunization has a negative and lasting impact on humoral immunity.
source: These results indicated that the presence of CD301b+ DCs during the early phase of primary immunization has a negative and lasting impact on humoral immunity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that early but not late depletion of CD301b+ DCs enhances antibody responses.

claim: CD301b+ DC-depleted mice generated robust antibody production against house dust mite after epicutaneous exposure.
source: Although this needle-free immunization protocol induced minimal amount of antibodies in WT mice even after multiple exposure to the antigen, CD301b+ DC-depleted mice generated robust antibody production (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f demonstrating enhanced antibody responses to HDM in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: Enhanced antibody responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice are found in response to subcutaneous papain immunization and to epicutaneous allergen exposure.
source: These results indicate that the enhanced antibody responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice are found in response to subcutaneous papain immunization and to epicutaneous allergen exposure.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data from both OVA/papain and HDM immunization experiments.

claim: CD301b+ DC-depleted animals showed a trend for enhanced antibody production after intraperitoneal immunization with OVA and alum.
source: We observed a trend for enhanced antibody production in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals, which was likely a result of the depletion of CD301b+ DC in the peritoneal cavity and its draining mediastinal LN (Kool et al., 2008) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and a citation to published literature (Kool et al., 2008).

claim: CD301b+ DCs in the peripheral organs expressed CD11b and MHCII but not Ly6C, but were nearly absent from the spleen.
source: As in the skin-dLNs, CD301b+ DCs in the peripheral organs expressed CD11b and MHCII but not Ly6C, but were nearly absent from the spleen (Figure 2c–f).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2c-f.

claim: In the skin-dLNs, the majority of CD301b+ cells were consistent with migratory DCs, as they were MHCIIhiCD11c+, CD64loLy6Clo, CD11b+CD11c+, CD24loCD11b+, and expressed a conventional DC marker Zbtb46.
source: In the skin-dLNs, the majority of CD301b+ cells were consistent with migratory DCs, as they were MHCIIhiCD11c+, CD64loLy6Clo, CD11b+CD11c+, CD24loCD11b+, and expressed a conventional DC marker Zbtb46 (Meredith et al., 2012; Satpathy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to published literature (Meredith et al., 2012; Satpathy et al., 2012).

claim: CD301b+ cells in the peritoneal cavity had a similar phenotype to those in skin-dLNs, though their Zbtb46 expression levels were lower.
source: CD301b+ cells in the peritoneal cavity had a similar phenotype, though their Zbtb46 expression levels were lower.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: DT treatment of Mgl2-DTR mice resulted in specific deletion of the CD301b+ DC subset, and did not grossly affect other cell types, except for an increase in the proportion of Ly6C+ cells in the peritoneal cavity.
source: The DT treatment of Mgl2-DTR mice resulted in specific deletion of the CD301b+ DC subset, and did not grossly affect other cell types, except for an increase in the proportion of Ly6C+ cells in the peritoneal cavity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD301b+ DCs constitute an important migratory DC population in skin and peritoneal cavity that negatively regulate antibody responses.
source: These results indicate that CD301b+ DCs constitute an important migratory DC population in skin and peritoneal cavity that negatively regulate antibody responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the characterization and functional data presented.

claim: Increasing doses of the antigen did not overcome suppression of antibody responses by CD301b+ DCs.
source: Increasing doses of the antigen did not overcome suppression of antibody responses by CD301b+ DCs (Figure 3b), indicating that limiting antigen access is not the dominant mode of antibody suppression by these DCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b demonstrating enhanced antibody responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice across different antigen doses.

claim: Limiting antigen access is not the dominant mode of antibody suppression by CD301b+ DCs.
source: Increasing doses of the antigen did not overcome suppression of antibody responses by CD301b+ DCs (Figure 3b), indicating that limiting antigen access is not the dominant mode of antibody suppression by these DCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that increasing antigen dose does not overcome suppression.

claim: CD301b+ DC-depleted mice developed strong antibody responses against OVA when immunized without any adjuvants.
source: Notably, CD301b+ DC-depleted mice developed strong antibody responses against OVA even when they were immunized without any adjuvants (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c demonstrating antibody responses to adjuvant-free OVA immunization.

claim: Materials released from dying CD301b+ DC cannot account for the enhanced antibody responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that materials released from dying CD301b+ DC cannot account for the enhanced antibody responses, and that lifting suppression by CD301b+ DCs enables induction of antibody to soluble protein antigens in the absence of adjuvants.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from bone marrow chimera experiments showing that WT CD301b+ DCs can suppress antibody responses even in the presence of dying Mgl2-DTR CD301b+ DCs.

claim: Lifting suppression by CD301b+ DCs enables induction of antibody to soluble protein antigens in the absence of adjuvants.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that materials released from dying CD301b+ DC cannot account for the enhanced antibody responses, and that lifting suppression by CD301b+ DCs enables induction of antibody to soluble protein antigens in the absence of adjuvants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing antibody responses to adjuvant-free immunization in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: CD301b+ DC-depleted animals produced higher levels of OVA-specific IgG2b after immunization with type 1 adjuvants CpG and LPS.
source: CD301b+ DC-depleted animals produced higher levels of OVA-specific IgG2b, suggesting that CD301b+ DCs also play a regulatory role in antibody production against type 1 antigens (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: CD301b+ DCs play a regulatory role in antibody production against type 1 antigens.
source: CD301b+ DC-depleted animals produced higher levels of OVA-specific IgG2b, suggesting that CD301b+ DCs also play a regulatory role in antibody production against type 1 antigens (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of enhanced IgG2b responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice immunized with type 1 adjuvants.

claim: Increasing the dose of CpG from 10 μg to 100 μg abrogated the difference in antibody levels between WT and CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
source: However, increasing the dose of CpG from 10 μg to 100 μg abrogated the difference in antibody levels between WT and CD301b+ DC-depleted mice (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The suppressive function of CD301b+ DCs can be overcome by the use of high dose type 1 adjuvants.
source: These results indicate that the suppressive function of CD301b+ DCs can be overcome by the use of high dose type 1 adjuvants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that high dose CpG eliminates the difference between WT and CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: The majority of the NP16OVA-specific antibodies produced in WT mice were directed to the hapten, as anti-OVA antibody responses were undetectable.
source: However, consistent with previous studies showing preferential development of hapten-specific rather than carrier-specific antibodies upon immunization with haptenated proteins (Palm and Medzhitov, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2007), the majority of the NP16OVA-specific antibodies produced in WT mice were directed to the hapten, as anti-OVA antibody responses were undetectable (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5b and citations to published studies (Palm and Medzhitov, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2007).

claim: CD301b+ DC-depleted mice developed significantly higher amount of antibodies against all epitopes examined including the OVA carrier.
source: In contrast, CD301b+ DC-depleted mice developed significantly higher amount of antibodies against all epitopes examined. Notably, unlike WT animals, CD301b+ DC-depleted mice also produced antibodies specific to the OVA carrier, indicating that the specificity of the antibodies were broadened in these mice (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The specificity of the antibodies were broadened in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
source: Notably, unlike WT animals, CD301b+ DC-depleted mice also produced antibodies specific to the OVA carrier, indicating that the specificity of the antibodies were broadened in these mice (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that CD301b+ DC-depleted mice produce antibodies to both hapten and carrier.

claim: Antibodies in immunized CD301b+ DC-depleted mice underwent similar (IgG1) or even slightly higher (IgG2b) levels of affinity maturation compared to the WT mice.
source: In addition, the ratio between the binding of the antibodies to bovine serum albumin (BSA) conjugated with high (NP34BSA) and low (NP4BSA) numbers of NP suggested that antibodies in immunized CD301b+ DC-depleted mice underwent similar (IgG1) or even slightly higher (IgG2b) levels of affinity maturation compared to the WT mice (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c measuring the NP4/NP34 binding ratio.

claim: CD301b+ DCs suppress the magnitude, breadth and affinity of antibodies.
source: These results indicate that CD301b+ DCs suppress the magnitude, breadth and affinity of antibodies.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on antibody magnitude, epitope breadth, and affinity maturation.

claim: Transient depletion of CD301b+ DCs for 9 days resulted in the development of anti-nuclear IgG antibodies 60 days later.
source: Indeed, transient depletion of CD301b+ DCs for 9 days resulted in the development of anti-nuclear IgG antibodies 60 days later (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 demonstrating anti-nuclear antibodies in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: CD301b+ DCs play a key role in suppressing the emergence of autoantibodies.
source: These results indicate that CD301b+ DCs play a key role in suppressing the emergence of autoantibodies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that transient depletion of CD301b+ DCs leads to autoreactive antibody development.

claim: The size of the dLNs at three days post-immunization in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals was much smaller than in undepleted controls, likely due to impaired screening and retention of naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: Consistent with our previous report, the size of the dLNs at three days post-immunization in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals was much smaller than in undepleted controls, likely due to impaired screening and retention of naïve CD4+ T cells (Kumamoto et al., 2013) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a,b and a citation to previous work (Kumamoto et al., 2013).

claim: The number of B cells in the dLNs started to increase on day five in the CD301b+ DC-depleted animals compared to the WT mice, which continued to increase until day seven.
source: However, the number of B cells in the dLNs started to increase on day five in the CD301b+ DC-depleted animals compared to the WT mice, which continued to increase until day seven (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The increase in the number of GC B cells was even more exaggerated than the increase in the number of total B cells in CD301b+ DC-deleted mice.
source: Consistent with the higher class-switched high-affinity antibody titers (Figures 1–3, 5), the increase in the number of GC B cells (CD95+ GL7+) was even more exaggerated than the increase in the number of total B cells in CD301b+ DC-deleted mice (Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 1e.

claim: In CD301b+ DC-depleted animals, an increased fraction of B cells that downregulated surface IgD receptor and bound to soluble fluorescently-labeled OVA protein was found, indicative of OVA-specific activated B cells.
source: In CD301b+ DC-depleted animals, an increased fraction of B cells that downregulated surface IgD receptor and bound to soluble fluorescently-labeled OVA protein was found, indicative of OVA-specific activated B cells (Figure 7d,f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d,f.

claim: An expansion of the CD38-GL7+ germinal center (GC) B cell fraction was observed in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice, while the CD38+GL7- naïve/memory fraction was significantly reduced.
source: We also observed an expansion of the CD38-GL7+ germinal center (GC) B cell fraction, while the CD38+GL7- naïve/memory fraction (Taylor et al., 2015) was significantly reduced (Figure 7h–j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7h-j and a citation to published literature (Taylor et al., 2015).

claim: OVA-specific B cells were preferentially enriched in the CD38-GL7+ GC B cell compartment in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
source: Notably, OVA-specific B cells were preferentially enriched in the CD38-GL7+ GC B cell compartment in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice (Figure 7h,k,l).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7h,k,l.

claim: The depletion of CD301b+ DCs induced antigen-specific B cells with a GC B cell phenotype in the dLNs.
source: These results indicate that the depletion of CD301b+ DCs induced antigen-specific B cells with a GC B cell phenotype in the dLNs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the B cell phenotyping data.

claim: CD4+ T cells of the Tfh phenotype (CXCR5+ PD-1+) were increased in number and frequency within the dLN of immunized CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
source: Indeed, CD4+ T cells of the Tfh phenotype (CXCR5+ PD-1+) were also increased in number (Figure 7—figure supplement 1d) and frequency (Figure 8a) within the dLN of immunized CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1d and Figure 8a.

claim: Among CD44hi effector CD4+ T cells, the ratio between PSGL1lo PD-1+ (follicular) cells to PSGL1hi PD-1- (extrafollicular) cells was significantly increased in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals compared to WT mice.
source: Similarly, among CD44hi effector CD4+ T cells, the ratio between PSGL1lo PD-1+ (follicular) cells to PSGL1hi PD-1- (extrafollicular) cells (Poholek et al., 2010) was significantly increased in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals compared to WT mice, further confirming the expansion of Tfh cells over other effector CD4+ T cells (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8b and a citation to published literature (Poholek et al., 2010).

claim: The accumulation of Tfh cells was selective to the canonical Tfh cells that express ICOS and Bcl6 and did not affect the follicular regulatory T (Tfr) cells.
source: The accumulation was selective to the canonical Tfh cells that express ICOS and Bcl6 and did not affect the follicular regulatory T (Tfr) cells (Figure 8c,d), suggesting that the increased GC B cell development was associated with the Tfh expansion rather than decrease in Tfr population.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: The increased GC B cell development was associated with the Tfh expansion rather than decrease in Tfr population.
source: The accumulation was selective to the canonical Tfh cells that express ICOS and Bcl6 and did not affect the follicular regulatory T (Tfr) cells (Figure 8c,d), suggesting that the increased GC B cell development was associated with the Tfh expansion rather than decrease in Tfr population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Tfh but not Tfr cells are increased in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: The increase in the Tfh fraction out of the total CD4+ T cells (significantly increased already by day five) preceded that of GC B cell increase (not significantly changed by day seven).
source: Interestingly, the increase in the Tfh fraction out of the total CD4+ T cells (significantly increased already by day five, Figure 8a) preceded that of GC B cell increase (not significantly changed by day seven, Figure 7b), suggesting that the depletion of CD301b+ DCs induced the Tfh accumulation, which resulted in GC B cell expansion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a and Figure 7b showing the temporal sequence of Tfh and GC B cell expansion.

claim: The depletion of CD301b+ DCs induced the Tfh accumulation, which resulted in GC B cell expansion.
source: Interestingly, the increase in the Tfh fraction out of the total CD4+ T cells (significantly increased already by day five, Figure 8a) preceded that of GC B cell increase (not significantly changed by day seven, Figure 7b), suggesting that the depletion of CD301b+ DCs induced the Tfh accumulation, which resulted in GC B cell expansion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal sequence of Tfh and GC B cell expansion.

claim: A larger fraction of OT-II CD4+ T cells differentiated into Tfh cells in CD301b+ DC-depleted hosts than in undepleted hosts.
source: A larger fraction of OT-II CD4+ T cells differentiated into Tfh cells in CD301b+ DC-depleted hosts than in undepleted hosts (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8e using adoptive transfer of OT-II cells.

claim: OT-II cells primed in the absence of CD301b+ DCs failed to differentiate into Th2 cells.
source: We previously reported OT-II cells primed in the absence of CD301b+ DCs failed to differentiate into Th2 cells (Kumamoto et al., 2013). Indeed, we observed reduced IL-4 production from CXCR5- OT-II effector T cells in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Kumamoto et al., 2013) and experimental data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: The expression levels (MFI) of IL-4 and IL-21 in CXCR5+ OT-II Tfh cells remained intact in CD301b+DC-depleted mice.
source: In fact, the expression levels (MFI) of IL-4 and IL-21 in CXCR5+ OT-II Tfh cells remained intact in CD301b+DC-depleted mice, while the percentages of IL-4- or IL-21-secreting OVA-specific Tfh (CXCR5+ OTII) increased (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8f measuring cytokine expression in Tfh cells.

claim: CD301b+ DC-depletion results in loss of Th2 cells but increase in Tfh cells capable of secreting IL-4 and IL-21.
source: These results indicate that CD301b+ DC-depletion results in loss of Th2 cells but increase in Tfh cells capable of secreting IL-4 and IL-21.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the cytokine expression data in different T cell subsets.

claim: The expansion of antigen-specific Tfh cells capable of secreting IL-4 and IL-21 underlies the enhanced type 2 antigen-specific antibody and GC B cell responses in the absence of CD301b+ DCs.
source: Further, our data suggest that the expansion of antigen-specific Tfh cells capable of secreting IL-4 and IL-21 underlies the enhanced type 2 antigen-specific antibody and GC B cell responses in the absence of CD301b+ DCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Tfh cells are increased and maintain cytokine production in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: Depletion of LCs did not result in enhanced OVA-specific antibody production.
source: Depletion of LCs did not result in enhanced OVA-specific antibody production (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9c using huLangerin-DTR mice.

claim: Depletion of all Langerin+ DCs (LCs and Langerin+ CD103+ DCs) in msLangerin-DTR mice had no impact on antibody responses.
source: Similarly, depletion of all Langerin+ DCs (LCs and Langerin+ CD103+ DCs) in msLangerin-DTR mice (Kissenpfennig et al., 2005; Poulin et al., 2007) had no impact on antibody responses (Figure 9d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9d and citations to published literature (Kissenpfennig et al., 2005; Poulin et al., 2007).

claim: DCs in general were required for B cell priming, as class-switched antibodies were completely abolished in CD11c-DTR;Mgl2-DTR mice.
source: Nevertheless, DCs in general were required for B cell priming, as class-switched antibodies were completely abolished in CD11c-DTR;Mgl2-DTR mice (Figure 9e), in which LN-resident DCs were further depleted (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9e and Figure 9—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: The antibody suppressive property is specific to the CD301b+ DCs and is not shared by other migratory DCs.
source: These results indicated that the antibody suppressive property is specific to the CD301b+ DCs and is not shared by other migratory DCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that depletion of other migratory DC subsets does not enhance antibody responses.

claim: Co-depletion of CD301b+ DCs, LCs and Langerin+ CD103+ DCs did not revert the enhanced antibody titers, Tfh, and GC B responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals despite near complete depletion of all migratory DC subsets.
source: Surprisingly, despite near complete depletion of all migratory DC subsets (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a,b), co-depletion of CD301b+ DCs, LCs and Langerin+ CD103+ DCs did not revert the enhanced antibody titers, Tfh, and GC B responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals (Figure 9c,d,f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9c,d,f and Figure 9—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Depleting Ly6C+ inflammatory monocyte-derived DCs concurrently with the CD301b+ DC depletion did not revert the expanded Tfh and GC cells.
source: Similarly, depleting Ly6C+ inflammatory monocyte-derived DCs concurrently with the CD301b+ DC depletion (Figure 9—figure supplement 1d) did not revert the expanded Tfh and GC cells (Figure 9g), suggesting that the potential increase in Ly6C+ cells in the periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) does not directly explain the phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9g and Figure 9—figure supplement 1d.

claim: CD301b+ DCs provide negative signals to Tfh precursors, while non-migrant DC population in the LN promotes Tfh differentiation, GC B and antibody responses.
source: These data are consistent with a model in which CD301b+ DCs provide negative signals to Tfh precursors, while non-migrant DC population in the LN promotes Tfh differentiation, GC B and antibody responses.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observation that migratory DC depletion does not reverse the phenotype while total DC depletion abolishes antibody responses.

claim: Within the non-lymphocyte population in the skin-dLNs, CD301b+ DCs express highest levels of both PD-1 ligands PD-L1 (B7-H1) and PD-L2.
source: Indeed, within the non-lymphocyte population in the skin-dLNs, CD301b+ DCs express highest levels of both PD-1 ligands PD-L1 (B7-H1) and PD-L2 (Figure 10a).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 10a.

claim: More than 90% of all PD-L1+ PD-L2+ non-lymphocytes were MHCIIhi migratory DCs, of which more than 40% consisted of CD301b+ DCs.
source: More than 90% of all PD-L1+ PD-L2+ non-lymphocytes were MHCIIhi migratory DCs, of which more than 40% consisted of CD301b+ DCs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 10a.

claim: In the dLN in WT mice, the PD-L1 but not PD-L2 blockade significantly enhanced the GC B cell and Tfh cell development.
source: In the dLN in WT mice, the PD-L1 but not PD-L2 blockade significantly enhanced the GC B cell and Tfh cell development (Figure 10c,d and Figure 10—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10c,d and Figure 10—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: In Mgl2-DTR mice, anti-PD-L1 blocking mAb did not exert further enhancement of the GC B cell and Tfh cell development.
source: In Mgl2-DTR mice, however, anti-PD-L1 blocking mAb did not exert further enhancement of the GC B cell and Tfh cell development (Figure 10c,d and Figure 10—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10c,d and Figure 10—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: PD-L1 in the residual cells does not have suppressive function on GCB or Tfh differentiation during priming.
source: Since PD-L1 expression was still intact in the residual DC subsets (Figure 10—figure supplement 1a), these data indicate that PD-L1 in the residual cells does not have suppressive function on GCB or Tfh differentiation during priming.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PD-L1 blockade does not enhance responses in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice despite PD-L1 expression on other cells.

claim: Antibody responses were enhanced by anti-PD-L1 antibody treatment only in the presence of CD301b+ DCs, whereas the PD-L2 blockade further increased OVA-specific IgG2b.
source: Consistent with the GC B cell expansion, antibody responses were enhanced by anti-PD-L1 antibody treatment only in the presence of CD301b+ DCs, whereas the PD-L2 blockade further increased OVA-specific IgG2b (Figure 10e,f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10e,f.

claim: Anti-PD-L1 blocking mAb enhances GC B cell responses in the dLNs by primarily targeting CD301b+ DCs in CD301b+ DC-intact animals.
source: These data indicate that anti-PD-L1 blocking mAb enhances GC B cell responses in the dLNs by primarily targeting CD301b+ DCs in CD301b+ DC-intact animals, and suggest that CD301b+ DCs use PD-L1 to control Tfh and GC B cell induction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PD-L1 blockade enhances responses only in the presence of CD301b+ DCs.

claim: CD301b+ DCs use PD-L1 to control Tfh and GC B cell induction.
source: These data indicate that anti-PD-L1 blocking mAb enhances GC B cell responses in the dLNs by primarily targeting CD301b+ DCs in CD301b+ DC-intact animals, and suggest that CD301b+ DCs use PD-L1 to control Tfh and GC B cell induction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PD-L1 blockade experiments showing CD301b+ DC-dependent effects.

claim: The increases in IgG2b responses by the PD-L2 blockade in the absence of CD301b+ DCs suggest a role for PD-L2 expressed on CD301b- cells in additionally suppressing humoral immunity.
source: In contrast, the increases in IgG2b responses by the PD-L2 blockade in the absence of CD301b+ DCs suggest a role for PD-L2 expressed on CD301b- cells in additionally suppressing humoral immunity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PD-L2 blockade enhances IgG2b responses even in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.

claim: Tfh and Th2 responses can be uncoupled, with the CD301b+ DCs as the pivotal cell type carrying out suppressive vs. supportive roles, respectively.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that, Tfh and Th2 responses can be uncoupled, with the CD301b+ DCs as the pivotal cell type carrying out suppressive vs. supportive roles, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that CD301b+ DCs suppress Tfh but promote Th2 responses.

claim: CD301b+ DC-mediated suppression occurs within the first few days of primary immune response, while the Tfr entry into the reactive LN occurs after 7 days of immunization.
source: CD301b+ DC-mediated suppression occurs within the first few days of primary immune response, while the Tfr entry into the reactive LN occurs after 7 days of immunization (Sage et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the timing experiments in this study and a citation to published literature (Sage et al., 2013).

claim: These two phases of Tfh regulation likely provide complementary mechanisms of Tfh control.
source: These two phases of Tfh regulation likely provide complementary mechanisms of Tfh control.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between CD301b+ DC-mediated and Tfr-mediated Tfh regulation.

claim: Regulation of Tfh responses at early phases by CD301b+ DCs may be critical in preventing excess antibody responses to foreign and self-antigens, which can lead to host pathology through complement fixation, and deposition of antibody-immune complex.
source: Regulation of Tfh responses at early phases by CD301b+ DCs may be critical in preventing excess antibody responses to foreign and self-antigens, which can lead to host pathology through complement fixation, and deposition of antibody-immune complex (Rouse and Sehrawat, 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance of CD301b+ DC-mediated regulation, supported by a citation about antibody-mediated pathology (Rouse and Sehrawat, 2010).

claim: CD301b+ DCs are the major subset of CD11b+ migratory DCs that most efficiently take up the antigen and bring to the dLNs within one day after immunization with papain.
source: CD301b+ DCs are the major subset of CD11b+ migratory DCs that most efficiently take up the antigen and bring to the dLNs within one day after immunization with papain.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge from previous studies by the authors.

claim: CD301b+ DCs are required for optimal screening and activation of naïve CD4+ T cells within the dLNs.
source: In addition, CD301b+ DCs are required for optimal screening and activation of naïve CD4+ T cells within the dLNs (Kumamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Kumamoto et al., 2013).

claim: Antibody responses against N. brasiliensis in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals are comparable to WT animals.
source: It is interesting, however, that antibody responses against N. brasiliensis in CD301b+ DC-depleted animals are comparable to WT animals (Kumamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Kumamoto et al., 2013).

claim: CD301b+ DCs did not suppress IgG2b antibody generated by strong type 1 immunity induced by high doses of CpG.
source: Similarly, CD301b+ DCs did not suppress IgG2b antibody generated by strong type 1 immunity induced by high doses of CpG (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Pathogens can overcome CD301b+ DC-dependent suppression of antibody responses, likely through continuous antigen presentation and through engagement of strong inductive signals through pattern recognition receptors including TLRs.
source: These results suggest that pathogens can overcome CD301b+ DC-dependent suppression of antibody responses, likely through continuous antigen presentation (Baumjohann et al., 2013; Deenick et al., 2010) and through engagement of strong inductive signals through pattern recognition receptors including TLRs (Pasare and Medzhitov, 2005).
evidence: This is speculation about how pathogens overcome CD301b+ DC suppression, supported by citations to relevant literature (Baumjohann et al., 2013; Deenick et al., 2010; Pasare and Medzhitov, 2005).

claim: The therapeutic effect of PD-L1 blockade in chronic infection by HIV and malaria is mediated in part by inducing more Tfh cells that help B cells to produce pathogen-specific neutralizing antibodies.
source: Recent studies have indicated that the therapeutic effect of PD-L1 blockade in chronic infection by HIV and malaria is mediated in part by inducing more Tfh cells that help B cells to produce pathogen-specific neutralizing antibodies (Butler et al., 2012; Cubas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Butler et al., 2012; Cubas et al., 2013).

claim: Continuous blockade as well as genetic deletion of PD-L1 was shown to enhance Tfh and GC B cell expansion upon type 2 immunization.
source: Similarly, continuous blockade as well as genetic deletion of PD-L1 was shown to enhance Tfh and GC B cell expansion upon type 2 immunization (Hams et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study (Hams et al., 2011).

claim: In previous studies with continuous PD-L1 blockade, activated B cells were the major source for the PD-L1 relevant to the memory Tfh population due to the timing of the PD-L1 blockade (past Tfh priming).
source: In these studies, due to the timing of the PD-L1 blockade (past Tfh priming), activated B cells were the major source for the PD-L1 relevant to the memory Tfh population.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism in previous studies based on the timing of intervention.

claim: The transient depletion of CD301b+ DCs during the priming phase had a significant positive impact on humoral immunity that persisted even after the secondary immunization.
source: In contrast, our results clearly demonstrated that the transient depletion of CD301b+ DCs during the priming phase had a significant positive impact on humoral immunity that persisted even after the secondary immunization.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings showing lasting effects of early CD301b+ DC depletion.

claim: Neonatal blockade of PD-L1 that is preferentially expressed by CD11b+ DCs in the lung results in exaggerated antibody production later in life during adulthood.
source: Consistently, a recent report demonstrated that neonatal blockade of PD-L1 that is preferentially expressed by CD11b+ DCs in the lung results in exaggerated antibody production later in life during adulthood, suggesting the contribution of a similar DC subset that suppresses humoral immunity through PD-L1 expression (Gollwitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study (Gollwitzer et al., 2014).

claim: GC B cell and IgG1 induction in response to NP-CGG immunization in PD-1 knockout mice are comparable or even slightly better than WT mice.
source: For instance, GC B cell and IgG1 induction in response to NP-CGG immunization in PD-1 knockout mice are comparable or even slightly better than WT mice (Good-Jacobson et al., 2010), consistent with our data.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study (Good-Jacobson et al., 2010).

claim: PD-1 deficient mice contain higher percentages of Tfr but not Tfh.
source: In contrast, the PD-1 deficient mice contain higher percentages of Tfr but not Tfh (Sage et al., 2013), and Tfh cells isolated from PD-1 deficient mice had impaired cytokine responses (Good-Jacobson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies (Sage et al., 2013; Good-Jacobson et al., 2010).

claim: Tfh cells isolated from PD-1 deficient mice had impaired cytokine responses.
source: In contrast, the PD-1 deficient mice contain higher percentages of Tfr but not Tfh (Sage et al., 2013), and Tfh cells isolated from PD-1 deficient mice had impaired cytokine responses (Good-Jacobson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study (Good-Jacobson et al., 2010).

claim: Autoreactive early immature B cells recognizing self-antigens are eliminated in the BM in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: Autoreactive early immature B cells recognizing self-antigens are eliminated in the BM in a cell-intrinsic manner.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about B cell central tolerance.

claim: Once in the periphery, mature B cells that react against autoantigens are suppressed by regulatory T cells (Tregs) in a cell-extrinsic manner.
source: Once in the periphery, mature B cells that react against autoantigens are suppressed by regulatory T cells (Tregs) in a cell-extrinsic manner (Meffre and Wardemann, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Meffre and Wardemann, 2008).

claim: The loss of B cell tolerance may be due to the emergence of self-reactive Tfh cells in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
source: Based on our analysis of protein antigen immunization in the absence of adjuvants, we believe that the loss of B cell tolerance may be due to the emergence of self-reactive Tfh cells in CD301b+ DC-depleted mice.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of autoantibody generation based on the experimental findings.
